title: I used AI to help build a TypeScript-to-SNES compiler and three Super Nintendo games. Here's the workflow that worked
author: vsgamesretro
selftext:
I'm a solo dev from Brazil making new games for the Super Nintendo that run on the real console. To do that I built SNES Studio, a browser app that compiles a subset of TypeScript to 65816 code, the SNES CPU.

  
AI was a big part of it, so here's how I used it honestly:

  
\- Code: AI wrote a lot of the typing, for the compiler passes, the runtime and the games. I owned the architecture, the language subset and every design call. The rule that kept it sane: the AI never got the last word, the hardware did. Every change was checked by building a ROM and running it in an emulator with test scripts.

\- Sound and text: AI helped with music drafts and with docs and devlog writing. All of it was edited by hand.

\- Balancing: for Tiny Run (a deckbuilder) I wrote bots that play thousands of runs with different decks and builds. That found balance problems I'd never have spotted by hand.

  
What surprised me:

1. A restricted language helps AI a lot. A small, documented subset (snes-studio.pages.dev/language) meant fewer made-up APIs and code that actually compiles for a 3.58 MHz CPU.

2. Tight limits (512 KB carts, 128 KB RAM) make AI output easy to check: it fits or it doesn't.

3. Benchmarks beat vibes. We keep a speed page (snes-studio.pages.dev/speed) comparing generated code with hand-written assembly; it currently sits around 1.04x.

  
It's free to try in the browser: https://snes-studio.pages.dev. Our three jam games (Super Wolf, Tiny Run, Space Blasting) are at https://vsgamesretro.itch.io.

  
Happy to answer questions about the workflow. What has worked for you when AI writes code for very constrained targets?
